newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Lupin fungus disease spreads in W. Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Lupin fungus disease spreads in W. Australia.

text.p: The lupin-killing fungus disease anthracnose had now been found in 13 crops in Western Australia (WA), a spokeswoman for the state farm authority Agriculture WA told Reuters.
All properties were being surveyed in the mid-west of the state, with the exercise expected to be finished by Thursday afternoon, she said.
Courses of action to combat the disease would then be determined, she said.

After apparently successful eradication measures of a single previous detection of the disease in WA in 1994, Australia had been regarded as one of the few anthracnose-free countries in the world until discovery of the disease on four WA properties last Thursday.
Initially, anthracnose eradication seemed like a very plausible prospect, the Agriculture WA spokeswoman said.
"Now that it's on 13 and, in fact, may be on more, they will have to assess how they are going to contain that," she said.
A statement would be made on Friday on what course of action had been decided on, she said.
Strategies had been put in place immediately to prevent spread of the disease and to make every effort to eradicate it, Agriculture WA's manager of pulses and oilseeds Rob Delane said in a statement.

There had been some talk of the worst diseased crops being destroyed but if anthracnose was very widespread eradication may possibly involve all seed being delivered at the end of the year, the department's spokeswoman said.
The Grain Pool of WA said in a statement on Wednesday that it had pledged full support and an initial A$20,000 to help contain the anthracnose outbreak.

Anthracnose was discovered in four Albus (white) lupin crops in the Geraldton region of WA last Thursday. It is a seed borne fungal disease that affects lupin crops and is transmitted within the crop by rain splash dispersal and movement of machinery, animals and people.
Grain Pool of WA general manager Kevin Swan said the outbreak of the disease could pose a serious threat to the A$200 million a year WA lupin industry.
"Our understanding is that there is no easy way to combat the disease once it is established other than not to plant lupins on the affected ground for up to four years," Swan said.
"From a marketing perspective we believe that careful monitoring of quality standards can minimise its impact on WA's major lupin markets," he said.
Anthracose, which forms an ulcerous fungus on lupin branches which then wilt, causing the plant to die, is common in Europe and most other producing countries.
Until last week, only Australia and South Africa were regarded as anthracnose-free.
The WA Grain Pool had sold lupins to South Africa in the past on a development basis but this had not involved significant tonnages, Swan said in today's statement.
Anthracnose has no ill effects on animals or humans who eat affected seed, Swan said.

In Australia, lupins are mainly used as stock feed. A small number of human consumption markets included Indonesia, but not Australia extensively, Andrew Young, manager communications and planning, at the Grain Pool, told Reuters.
In Australia, lupins are used in aquaculture, stockfeed, poultry, pig and cattle feed, he said.
WA is Australia's leading lupin producing state.
